props.title: Dangerous Men

sections.content: **Dangerous Men (2005)** (2005) stands as one of the most fascinatingly inept films ever made, joining the ranks of celebrated "so-bad-they're-good" classics like **The Room** (2003) and **Troll 2** (1990). Shot piecemeal over two decades by Iranian-American filmmaker John S. Rad, this revenge thriller defies conventional filmmaking logic at every turn. The plot, if you can call it such, follows a woman seeking vengeance after bikers kill her fiancé, but spirals into incomprehensible subplots involving ninja cops, random musical numbers, and extended scenes of characters doing mundane tasks.

sections.content: What makes **Dangerous Men** particularly remarkable is its place in the pantheon of outsider cinema. Like **Plan 9 from Outer Space** (1959) and **Manos: The Hands of Fate** (1966), it represents pure, unfiltered artistic vision - albeit one completely divorced from basic filmmaking competence. The editing jumps between scenes filmed decades apart, actors change appearance mid-scene, and the sound mixing ranges from inaudible to deafening. Yet there's an undeniable earnestness that elevates it above simple "bad movie" status.

The film's release history mirrors other cult phenomena like **The Room** (2003). After spending nearly $1 million of his own money over 26 years of production, Rad briefly released it in 2005 to empty theaters before it was rediscovered and championed by exploitation film preservationists Drafthouse Films in 2015. This positions it alongside other rescued obscurities like Miami Connection (1987) and **Roar** (1981) as examples of pure outsider art finding appreciation decades after their creation. SUBHEAD: The Technical Magnificence of Failure

The technical aspects of **Dangerous Men** deserve special attention for their consistent ability to break every established rule of cinema. The fight scenes appear to have been filmed by someone who had never seen actual combat or watched an action movie. Sound effects drop out entirely or arrive several seconds after the action they're meant to accompany. Most remarkably, the film's score - composed by Rad himself - seems to have been created without any regard for what's happening onscreen, leading to upbeat synthesizer music during tragic deaths and ominous drones during casual conversations.
